When this estimate was before the committee on the last occasion there was some discussion of fish traps in British Columbia, and I would refer again briefly to that matter. I do not propose to rehash the whole subject. It would take hours and the matter would be unsuitable for a committee of this size. That is why a special committee was instituted for the discussion of all such matters. To-day I simply want, so to speak, to begin where the committee left off. The committee submitted a report, the first recommendation of which reads:
That no more trap licences be granted in British Columbia waters except in the so called Sooke area, and concerning which we are unable to come to a decision as to whether they should be continued or not, without the opportunity of securing further information.

Supply-Fisheries
There were some other recommendations, and the last one indicates that a check should be made on fish caught and the details carefully collected. I maintain that the report in its essence, although the word was not used, was an interim report. It was so regarded by the committee. It stated that the committee were unable to come to a decision as to whether the whole matter referred to them should be decided or not without opportunity of securing further information, and they recommended that the department should secure that additional information. Some of that information has been obtained and I have it here now. Speaking on this subject, the minister made a statement which I wish to quote. I asked that the data which the committee had recommended should be collected, and which had been collected, should be referred to the committee, and the minister made this statement:
Mr. Michaud:	That is a matter which my
hon. friend should refer either to the house or to the committee. As far as the department is concerned, the recommendations made last year by the committee were carried out. I feel that is all that should be expected of the minister or the department.
Dealing with the first sentence, I would point out that it was impossible for me to refer the matter to the committee because a private member cannot refer a matter to a committee without the consent of the minister concerned, and that was lacking. I had written and asked him whether he would refer it to the committee and he refused. To say that I can refer it to the house means that I can bring it up only now when conditions are not favourable for a detailed debate. I would call attention especially to the remarkable sentence in which the minister says that all that can be expected of the minister of a department is to carry out the recommendations made. That, to my mind, illustrates a distinct failure to appreciate the purpose of the investigation, which was to decide whether we should continue the use of fish traps in British Columbia, and we decided in our wisdom that we could not make that decision for lack of further information. The minister now proposes to rest on his oars and say that he has done all that he was asked to do and will not do any more. At page 2297 of Hansard it will be seen that I sent the minister a letter asking him whether he would refer the matter to the committee or stop the traps, and he replied that he would do neither. I think it is very much up to the minister to inform this committee to-day why he refused to comply with the terms of a numerously signed petition presented to the house, or, 51952-199
failing that, if he deemed that the matter was not thoroughly threshed out, why he did not refer it again to the committee. Why did he refuse to have the matter referred to the committee and in that way close it out entirely from further debate? I would ask him for an explanation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext: There are two aspects of this question in which my hon. friend is interested. The first is the question of the petitions which he laid on the table of the house shortly after the opening of parliament, and the second is the report of the special committee which sat during last session. The reason why the department did not take the initiative and refer again to the committee the whole question of the advisability of discontinuing the issuing of licences for fish traps in the Sooke area of British Columbia, and the matter of the petitions, is that since last session no new facts have been brought to my attention, no new evidence which would have justified me in asking for the committee to sit again this year to consider the matter. It is true that we had petitions; but in those petitions there were no new facts disclosed which had not been brought to the attention of the department some years ago and which have not, from year to year since, been submitted to us. The facts which were gathered by the department during the recess, at the request of the committee, were brought to my notice, and I did not think they disclosed anything different from what had been submitted to the committee last year and had been discussed for a considerable time, forming the basis of the committee's report. So that if the hon. member was in possession of some new evidence, I think it was up to him either to bring it to the attention of the house or to ask that the committee be called together
I did.

and the matter brought before the committee. My hon. friend says he did. If I remember rightly, he asked me in a letter whether the petitions which were submitted by him to the house would be referred to a committee, and I replied that in view of the fact that the petitions disclosed no new facts I did not think it my business to call the committee again to deal with a matter that had been dealt with last year.
As to the data collected by the department during the recess, I never understood that my hon. friend asked me to refer it to the fisheries committee, and this is the first time that I understand he intended to have this

Supply-Fisheries

data, passed on to him at his own request, referred to the committee, because, as I said before, in my opinion it did not seem to disclose any new facts upon which the committee would be justified in changing the recommendations they made last year.

The minister says that he did not refer the matter to the committee because there was not new evidence which in his opinion justified its being referred to them. But I humbly submit that there was new evidence, and I have it under my hand. One of the main questions brought up in the committee was as to the number of fish caught, the varieties and so on. The contention on both sides centred repeatedly on that point- exactly what was caught in those traps-and we recommended that information should be obtained as to what was caught, And that information was obtained, because I have it before me, and in my humble opinion it constitutes new evidence if anything could be called new evidence, because it was something that was not before the committee previously. The minister says that no new evidence was disclosed-in his opinion. But the matter has gone beyond the question of his opinion. A committee was appointed to consider the matter, and that committee was entitled to go on and conclude it. The minister says that I did not ask that the matter be referred.

I did not make that
statement. I said that I did not understand my hon. friend to request that this particular evidence should be referred to the committee.

Not this particular evidence, but all of it. I have here the letter I wrote, and I have what the minister said. He guards himself by a general statement-he is not sure. Well, he knew that the estimates were coming down to-day and that the matter would be brought up. I venture to say that my letter is before him at this moment. Then he makes statements that give a wrong impression of my letter. This is my letter, dated February 28-long enough ago: Honourable J. E. Michaud,
Minister of Fisheries,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Michaud:
With reference to the question of fish traps at Sooke, _ you will recall that the report of the committee last year stated that we leave the question of traps at Sooke open for further consideration.
Since then, I presented a petition the other day containing nearly 10,000 names, and I still have petitions coming in asking for their abolition.
Might I inquire what your policy in the matter is? Are you disposed to give them notice-

That is, the trap owners.
-that they will not be allowed any for or beyond this year, or do you propose to refer it again to the fisheries committee of the house?
The minister replied that he was not going to do either one or the other. How I could have put it more plainly I cannot conceive, or how he could have stated more definitely that he was not going to do it. The fact remains that the minister has not allowed the matter to go to the committee. There was new evidence, evidence that was not before us before. Did we have any evidence before- I ask any member of the committee-that whales had been caught in the traps last year or ratfish or porpoises? We had this new information, and the totals of salmon caught, and it should have been submitted to the committee. There the matter ends so far as I am concerned at the moment. I am not going to prolong this debate indefinitely, and the committee would not be interested. But I charge the Department of Fisheries with straight neglect of duty in this matter, and there I leave it, for the issue to go before a higher tribunal, perhaps.
There is another matter in connection with fish traps which is more important and which touches to a certain degree the honour of this house. My information is not simply something I have heard, but what the minister himself says. Speaking in the house on April 26 last, he referred to these petitions about which I spoke, and then he said, as reported at page 2296 of Hansard :
Some petitions containing the same heading were forwarded to my office, I suppose inadvertently. These contained the post office addresses and occupations of the people who signed them and I found that they contained the signatures of more chicken farmers than fishermen.
And I replied:
Certainly.
The reason is that the population of British Columbia was much greater than that of the fishermen, and the people who would sign the petition would naturally be more numerous than the numbers of the fishermen because the petition was signed by the residents of British Columbia. The point I draw to the attention of the committee is this, and I would draw it to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is leading the government. The hon. Minister of Fisheries admitted the receipt of some of the petitions with the same heading. I have the petition here. It is addressed, "To the Honourable House of Commons in Parliament Assembled." That is, it is addressed to only one body, and that is the body sitting here.

S upply-Fishe ries
It is the law, is it not, Mr. Chairman, that when letters are inadvertently delivered to the wrong person they shall be immediately handed over to the person to whom they were addressed? There are three members of this house with names very similar: O'Neill, Mac-Neil and Neill, and in the course of time, perhaps through the carelessness of clerks or because of the letters being wrongly directed, we get each other's mail. But I would be astonished if anyone suggested that we did not, all three of us, immediately turn such letters over to the person for whom they were intended and who owned them. Postal rule 244, I think it is, lays down that a letter once posted is the property of the person to whom it is addressed. The minister says himself that he got a number of these petitions. I do not know how many but I did have a kind of sneaking suspicion that something of that kind had happened because copies of some of the petitions I had sent out seemed to be missing. I have always and ever maintained that the proper plan of spending money on fishing is not to spend it in the offices in the Hunter block, or in Vancouver-and particularly in Vancouver-but to spend it on the grounds in preventing poaching; because one can go in at night and in a few hours undo the good the department has done in three or four years. A man may put a net across the mouth of a little river or creek and clean it out. The result is that next year, instead of the fish going up by thousands they go up by scores, and it takes four or five years to regain the run. Therefore I say it does not pay to preserve a fish run for three or four years and then, through lack of a guardian at a particular point, to allow a poacher to come in and destroy what has been done. I say that because people will poach, and it is inevitable that if they are given the opportunity they will clean up the river. So I say as long as the money is spent on fish guardians, more power to them, because they are doing real good. Has Canada delegated to Olympia the right to legislate for Canada in this or any other matter, and must Canada confine its fishing operations to gear to which Americans have no objection? of the fishermen of Puget sound. Certainly, however, the mere fact that for the past two or three years its proportion of the catch has shown some improvement should occasion no qualms of conscience on the part of Canada.
When the member for Comox-Alberni originally made the statement on the floor of the house that traps were the most destructive form of fishing, as they fish day and night, while every practical fisherman knew it to be untrue, the member was given the benefit of the doubt and it was assumed that the statement was made from ignorance or misinformation. At the committee hearings at Ottawa last winter, however, this error was pointed out and since that date the member has had ample time to correct his misstatement. When he now sponsors a repetition of this falsehood, he leaves no alternative than to believe that lie does so deliberately and wilfully.
I am sorry, but that is in this statement.
Traps do not fish day and night in British Columbia or elsewhere. The Sooke trap nets are so constructed that they fish only on the flood tide, and they can fish effectively only from four to six hours even in daylight. Phosphorus in the water makes night fishing out of the question and traps are invariably closed during the hours of darkness. As to the statement that nothing escapes the trap or gets through, fish once taken by any type of gear are not expected to get through. However, about 98 per cent of the fish get by as shown by the records.
Records of the catches of springs and cohoes, while not as complete as the records of sock-e.ves show conclusively that the proportion of the total catch of these varieties taken by the Sooke traps is not far different from that of sockeyes.
Nothing justifies the statement that abolition of traps would lead to any increase in employment, but on the contrary, it is definitely known that it would immediately result in throwing out of employment forty or fifty men now profitably employed at Sooke, owning in most cases their own homes and knowing no other means of livelihood. It would be simply a case of a repetition of the old fable of the dog dropping his bone to grasp at its reflection in the water.
Tourist fishermen now find the local waters an attractive field for sport fishing. During the past season many excellent catches were made. These were principally the spring and eolioe salmon.

This entire trap net question was thoroughly investigated last winter by the fisheries committee at Ottawa, and the opponents of trap nets were given every opportunity of presenting their case. Referring later to the fact stated in the petition, that the associated boards of trade of Vancouver island had voted against fish traps, I have this letter dated February 28, 1938, in reply to my statement, from the same gentleman, Mr. Charles F. Goodrich, of the Sooke Harbour Fishing and Packing Company, Limited, Victoria, British Columbia:
We note that Mr. Neill states that this petition was signed by Mr. W. W. R. Mitchell, president of the associated boards of trade of Vancouver island and 9,594 others, "all citizens of British Columbia."
The reference to Mr. Mitchell's office is entirely gratuitous. He was never authorized by the associated boards of trade to sign in his official capacity. It is true that a resolution against trap nets was railroaded through at a meeting of the associated boards at

Nanaimo at Mr. Neill's instigation last June in violation of the rules previously adopted governing such matters. Then follows other matter, which is at the disposal of any inquiring member of the committee.
This is really a very serious matter, and it should not be hastily judged by hon. members in committee. They should go into the whole matter very seriously, because, as I tried to point out to the committee last year, it in-, volves the life history of the various types of salmon, which in turn involves an understanding of the biological history of these fish, and unless one can see precisely what is going on it is useless to attempt to decide whether or not traps or trap nets should be abolished at this particular point. They were established at Sooke after long and close investigation some twenty-five years or more ago, and they have remained there because of the peculiar strategic condition which obtains at that point. The strait of Juan de Fuca is approximately eighty miles long, and varies in width from ten to eighteen miles, having an average width of, say twelve miles. Hon. members can reduce that strait to the compass of this house, which is ninety-two feet long between doors and sixty-one feet wide between panels beyond the curtains. If you then take lour and a half lengths of this house you have the length of the strait, with the width of the house as the width of the strait, roughly speaking. All these trap nets occupy a space within half the length of this house. The shortest of them is no longer by comparison than the length of a man's hand, and the longest of them, 2,000 feet, is no longer than the length of a man's arm. So, if you can visualize in the width of this house the length of a man's arm stretching out from the panels at the wall, you visualize the longest trap in its relationship to the width of Juan de Fuca strait. If you visualize the length of a man's hand sticking out from the panels, you can see what is the obstruction in the strait of the shortest trap net at Sooke. These things are worth noting. All that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said is not proof to a discerning individual that these traps should be abolished.
He made quite a joke of the fact that a whale was caught in these traps. Surely; a whale would be caught in any net strong 
enough to catch him, and if we say that all kinds of fish were caught in the traps that is equally true of all kinds of fishing gear. Very, very rarely when fish are running are they running pure to type. There is always an admixture; there are always camp followers, always fish of other types than those running. But the peculiar feature of the whole thing is that in the eighty mile stretch of the strait there comes a point at which fifty miles from the entrance the salmon leave their general run and turn south in order to pass down into Puget sound. The Juan de Fuca strait runs practically east for fifty miles and then makes a sudden turn to east northeast, and it is at that point of departure that for some reason or another the fish turn down into United States waters. It was for this reason that the traps were permitted to be constructed at Sooke, roughly speaking, in the first instance. What causes the fish to go down there I have not been able to discover; but the chances are that inasmuch as they have, roughly speaking, 150 to 250 miles to travel before they reach the mouth of the Fraser river, it may be conceded that they are not yet ready to enter fresh water, and that immediately they taste the fresh water from the Fraser river, which throws its influence right away down, they turn off into the salt water leading down into Puget sound. Whether or not this is so, the fact remains that this change of direction into United States waters gives the fishermen their chance, and gives the traps their opportunity. These traps in United States waters are not like the traps at Sooke, for they are planted quite definitely in the shallow channels between the various islands.

I observed that, I think for the first time,

It would be impossible and highly undesirable for me to go all over the ground my hon. friend covered; but I want to say that the great bulk of his presentation to-night was an ex parte statement drawn up probably by a lawyer but at least sent to him by the very man whose interests are so vitally at stake, Mr. Goodrich, and Mr. Goodrich has an enormous interest at stake, because he is in possession of an enormous privilege belonging to the people of Canada, out of which he is making a whale of a lot of money. Naturally he will draw up a statement that at least will look plausible as against this petition. But he had his chance before the committee, and there he showed up very differently from the fancy picture he draws in the letter which has been read to the committee to-night. He repeatedly contradicted himself. Frequently he said, "I will not tell that." "Do I have to tell that?" Finally he admitted that he paid an income tax so large that it was very easy to figure the profits of that company. He was asked whether these things were true. My hon. friend went on to make the statement that the traps did not fish at night. They do fish day and night; they fish whenever the tide is most suitable, as any other fisherman does. They can fish twenty-four hours a day, and it is not correct to say they are closed at night, because they are not. If they are closed at all, it is only because of the weekly forty-eight hour requirement of the dominion government.

Then my hon. friend said we would throw a lot of people out of employment. He knows better than that; he is not doing himself justice when he makes that statement. At the very most it would throw forty-one people out of employment, the people who signed the petition as employees of the company, who naturally do not want to lose their jobs. But man after man rose and stated that it would enormously increase the employment of fishermen if these traps were done away with. A member of the committee-I shall not mention his name, because I know he is a modest man-rose and said, "I am getting a little tired of this line of talk. I own a cannery, as you all know. If I could have a trap at my door, the same as these gentlemen have, I would only employ from twelve to fifteen men a year, whereas now I have to employ between 200 and 400. But I am willing to do it because I am giving employment to fishermen. "But," he said, "I do feel like asking this: If this gentleman has to have a trap, why should not the other thirty-eight canneries which do not have traps also have them?"
That is on record in Hansard. Then the hon. member said the arguments advanced against traps were entirely unconvincing. Were they? That is remarkable, is it not? Yet we presented a report-he says so himself-recommending that the licence fees should be raised from $50. They had seven licences. They did not use them all, but they hogged them to prevent anybody else from using them. Those seven licences they obtained at $50 each, making a total of $350. We recommended that the fee be raised from $50 per licence to $500, and they did not make any objection. They were glad to pay that enormous increase. I do not know whether my figures of percentages are correct or not; it is a 1,000 per cent increase. if my figures are correct. Anyway it is certainly a great increase, from a total of $350 to one of $3,500, and they did not make a chirp of objection. They were only too glad to get away with it at that price, when they were getting this enormous privilege from the people of Canada. We were getting $350 out of them, and we were paying an overseer about $700 to look after matters. Now we are getting $3,500.
The hon. member says one of the things misstated in the petition was that the associated boards of trade at Vancouver Island at their annual meeting in June last passed a resolution asking for the abolition of the traps. That is actually and entirely true and can be easily and regularly proved. The hon. member's ignorance on that point is as great

as his ignorance on the point as to where the meeting was held. He says it was held at Nanaimo, and it was actually held at Port Alberni. He tells what took place. I was there and he was not; I know what happened, and as God is my witness I shall give the exact facts.
There was a resolution on the agenda of the meeting of the associated boards of trade of Vancouver island, and that resolution dealt with traps. The custom or the rale is to circulate the agenda beforehand, and that resolution was circulated with the rest. But even if it is alleged that it was not on the agenda-and it was; it was certainly on the one we used at the meeting-it was made official at any rate by the credentials committee which adopted it, and passed it unanimously and without protest.
The resolution was brought up in the meeting. There were two delegates at the meeting from the Victoria chamber of commerce; there may have been more, but I know that there were at least two of them. When the resolution was brought up, one of those gentlemen rose and said, "There is a point about this thing I am not quite clear on." He might have said more than that; but I do know that was said, and he indicated that he wanted further knowledge. The chairman said, "Mr. Neill is in the audience; he is familiar with the situation and can give the information you wish." I asked what he wanted to know. Replying to him I spoke only a few moments, and before anything further could be done that same man said "Carried," and the resolution went through unanimously. There were no other protests whatever.
Then the traps interests got busy. They have powerful interests in Victoria, and they got the chamber of commerce to repudiate the action of their delegates. They said that the delegates had no business to do as they had done, because they had been told not to vote on anything of a controversial nature. The matters could not have been very controversial, because the vote was carried unanimously, and there was no objection other than the one I have stated.
Then they got busy. In the interim there was a semi-annual meeting of the executive, and it was said that if they did not repudiate the action of the associated boards of trade -which they were not able to do, because they were only the executive-the Victoria chamber would withdraw from the affiliated boards. In other words, "If I don't get my way I won't play in your back-yard." It is not the first time that the Victoria chamber have adopted that hoggish attitude if they

do not get everything their way. It would not hurt the rest of us on Vancouver island one little bit if they did withdraw. We would get along better without them. Have I been one? If I were a sockeye I would

Certainly we are. But when false arguments are put forward by an hon. member, I have, I think, a right to dissect them. I was not talking to the hon. member at all. I was speaking about his arguments concerning the percentage of lead compared with the width of the straits. As I say, if he were familiar with the habits of sockeye he would know something about its homing instinct. It spawns, goes to sea and stays there four years. At the end of that period, in spite of hell and high water, it will come back again, and it will go to only one place; it will go back to the place where it was spawned and it will go nowhere else. It will not go ten or twelve miles away to another stream, but it will come right back to where it was spawned. It is a biological urge within it which comes on at the end of four or five years.
These traps are put out at the good headlands, where the fish will come around the headlands. If I were going around the corner of that table and wished to go to the minister's seat, I would not go around by the seat of the hon. member for Nanaimo, would I? I would have all that width, if I wished to use it, but naturally if I were walking to the minister's seat I would do as I would if driving a car. I would hug the right-hand corner, or keep to the right of the road. That is exactly what the fish do. They go to the headland, and when they go to the right they find a piece of wire-netting sticking out. They cannot go up on the shore; so they go along in the opposite direction, poking along, until they come to the trap. That is the end of it. Of course they could back up and go out to sea, but it is not their custom-and you cannot make a salmon do something different from its natural instinct, or different from that which nature intended it to do. That is the explanation of the percentage.
Then, although I did not hear him accurately, I believe he was reading from a reprint of a Pacific coast fishing newspaper, a memorandum or a brochure got out in the early spring dealing with various matters in connection with Fraser river salmon and, incidentally, with other matters as well. but considering that a large proportion of that pamphlet was in the direction of continuing the fish traps, one might perhaps make an invidious suggestion. It was written

I am at a loss to understand the attitude of the minister in denying us an opportunity to continue the investigation initiated last session. I was one of the members who wrote to the minister urging that course earlier in this session, and I resent very much the remark he made this afternoon. The minister stated that it was the privilege of hon. members of the committee who were not satisfied with his attitude to call the matter to the attention of the chairman of the committee for some definite action. I think the minister is aware, as we are, that the chairman of the committee has acted with strict impartiality and unfailing courtesy in connection with this matter, but he could not very well act in the matter unless reference had been made to the committtee by the house with the sanction of the government.
I am at a complete loss to understand why the minister has disregarded the intentions of the committee which sat last year. It' is

Supply-Fisheries
true the findings of the committee were inconclusive as to whether the traps at Sooke should be abolished, but it was clearly understood that further evidence would be procured through the department and that the members of the committee would be afforded an opportunity to settle this matter in a more satisfactory way. Hon. members have stated on their responsibility as members of this house that these traps were a menace to the fishing industry of British Columbia, and it is hardly good enough to hear the minister say, as he said this afternoon, that the additional evidence and the expression of public opinion in the petition were not sufficiently worth while to justify further investigation.
May I point out that the further evidence required is strictly of a technical nature and that it can be obtained only from the experts in the employ of the department. It was understood that they would continue the investigation and make that information available so that this matter might be settled in some judicial fashion. Evidence has been submitted that two companies are enjoying a privilege or a monopoly at the expense of the workers in the industry, workers who must face daily hazards to get the slender remuneration they receive for their labours. I consider the attitude of the minister in this regard to be rather high-handed. We have the unique spectacle in this issue where he extends special protection to privileged interests, to two companies, to exploit the resources of the Dominion of Canada with enormous profits to themselves and disregard the welfare of the workers dependent upon the industry.
In past years the Department of Fisheries has followed the excellent practice of giving the organized workers in the industry an opportunity to discuss any contemplated changes in the regulations. The workers have been permitted to advance their views as to how the proposed changes might affect their interests. But in this particular instance the minister has broken faith with the workers in order to protect these two companies which enjoy a special privilege which menaces the fishing industry of British Columbia. When I say the industry in British Columbia, I mean the very livelihood of thousands of fishermen. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that this is a clear illustration of protection for monopoly on the part of a government department with a total disregard of the interests of the workers. It i3 a menace to the livelihood of the workers.
Two companies established at Sooke, with quite a large capital investment, have been 51952-200
fishing with fixed traps, that is traps which are fixed to shore, a privilege denied the operators of all other types of gear and in violation of well established principles of conservation of the industry. A very definite effort has been made to secure the cooperation of all sections to maintain these principles of conservation as expressed in the regulations of the department, and it is extremely difficult to advocate the support of these principles when we have this glaring illustration of protection of operations which do definitely violate the principles of cor servation of the fishing industry. It is ' menace to the livelihood of the workers u the industry, because it affords a pretext to interests in the state of Washington to reestablish traps in United States waters where they can successfully intercept the main movement of sockeye salmon into the Fraser river.
As has been mentioned, on one occasion a widespread agitation was under way for the repeal of legislation in the state of Washington and leading to the reestablishment of traps there. If those traps are established in United States waters, this will deal a most disastrous blow to the fishermen who depend for their livelihood upon gill netting in the Fraser river. In my opinion, if this privilege is now extended to the two companies established at Sooke, there is no logical reason why other companies should not be later afforded the same privilege of establishing traps at strategic points in the coastal waters of British Columbia; and if that is done, it will completely wipe out the livelihood of many thousands of fishermen in that province.
For those three main reasons the continued operation of these traps is a distinct threat to the industry. The minister, in the attitude he has taken, I think has broken faith with the members of the committee and with the workers in the industry in order to protect those special interests. There is nothing more at stake at Sooke than the employment of forty men. Those forty men, as experienced fishermen, could easily be absorbed in other branches of the fishing industry. The capital invested at Sooke could easily be diverted to other types of operations such as purse seining in other waters. No distinct hardship would result if the minister decided to discontinue the issuance of licences for the fish traps at Sooke, and I think the minister owes this committee a more adequate explanation than he has yet given as to why he has not seen fit to refer this matter to the committee for thorough inquiry, place at the disposal of the committee the additional technical evidence

which might have been procured, and enable a satisfactory settlement of this issue to be made.
It is not good enough to speak with derision of that petition. I have some knowledge of the circumstances under which signatures were obtained to it. It is true they are not all signatures of fishermen, but to a very large extent they are signatures of people in communities which depend in very large measure upon the prosperity of the fishing industry and realize the menace of the fishing traps. The minister cannot hope to dispose of the question in the way in which he has attempted to do so this afternoon. Public sentiment is aroused through these communities as to this issue, and will ultimately demand a more satisfactory settlement. I urge the minister to take steps to have this matter brought before the standing fisheries committee at some appropriate time and have it investigated thoroughly in the light of the technical evidence that his department is in a position to procure.

Even though
some of the members of the committee had requested that it should be convened, I think my hon. friend will appreciate the position in which I, as chairman, would be. Will the hon. member for Vancouver North permit a question? On the Swiftsure banks outside the strait of Juan de Fuca, fifty-two United States purse seiners sit and fish. I think the answer is fairly simple. Canadian operators have enjoyed the special privilege, with less effort and less expense, to establish six traps at Sooke, and none of the Canadian operators has had the enterprise indicated by the United States operators to construct and operate the type of craft which could successfully fish off the Swiftsure banks.

Before we proceed any further on this point, I wish to repudiate the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver North, that the minister "broke

faith" with the committee or did not carry out the directions of the committee. Second, there was no refusal on my part at any time to refer the matter to the committee. What took place is this, that I think both the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Vancouver North wrote asking me if I would refer to the committee the petitions that were presented to the house. That is my recollection of it.
Will the minister permit an interruption?
Yes.

My suggestion was that
the whole question, a continuation of the inquiry of last year, should be referred to the committee.

Yes, and I think I replied to both gentlemen that, in my opinion, nothing new had been brought to my attention or no new evidence or facts placed before the department which would justify me in my capacity as minister to take the initiative of calling together the committee and referring matters which, in my opinion, had been thoroughly investigated last year. If either of these two hon. members or any member of the house had asked me to refer a special matter to the committee, I could not have refused him that privilege because it was not in my power to do so. There was no intention on my part or on the part of the department to prevent anybody from bringing to the attention of parliament through the committee any new matter respecting the question of fish traps in British Columbia. This is not a new matter. There have been fish traps at Sooke for thirty-four years.
Too long.

All governments prior
to this year have received at different times petitions and requests for the removal of those traps, and the best opinions have been taken into consideration. It has not been thought it was in the best interests of the fisheries to do that, and until such a conclusion is warranted I do not think any minister will take the responsibility of changing an order of things which has been going on for thirty-four years. It might be in the interests of some branch of the fisheries on the coast of British Columbia to remove the traps; but as I said, they have never been able yet to convince me, and they have never been able

Supply-Fisheries
to convince any of my predecessors for the last thirty-four years, that it was in the best interests of the industry to remove those traps. Any hon. member besides the hon. members for Comox-Alberni and Vancouver North could have had the matter referred to the committee when these petitions were laid on the table of the house; they could have moved, if they had desired to do so, that these petitions be referred to the committee on fisheries for investigation and further inquiry. I would have raised no objection. As I said before, I have no objection whatever, and it is not in my power to raise any. Indeed, it is not too late now. Why do not these hon. members do it? I shall not take the responsibility for calling the committee together again to go over matters which, in my opinion, were thoroughly gone into last year. If any hon. member has any new matter which he thinks ought to be considered, it is for him to ask that the committee be called together. I would be delighted to appear before the committee and listen to any arguments advanced and to carry out any recommendations made, just as we carried out the recommendations that were made last year.
The minister has made one statement which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. He said that these things have been going on for over thirty-four years. Is that correct?
That is my information -that there have been traps there since 1904.

Yes. Well, for some periods
during that time-for many periods in fact -I made no objection to the traps being there. But surely the minister knows the reason why the agitation was started. As we are threshing this matter out, very regrettably I shall have to give the history of it. There has always been, an agitation by the cannery men for traps, because they are a quick and effective way of catching fish, though disastrous to the fishermen and the fish alike. From 1907 onward this question has cropped up from time to time. There were traps at Sooke and other places; some time around 1924 or 1925 or 1926 the cannery men conceived the idea that they would like to have traps in the northern part of British Columbia, and so they got a commissioner appointed, a gentleman who- had been a lawyer for one of the canning companies. He went there and made an elaborate report. He reported that the run of fish was such that it was highly in the interests of Canada to allow traps there because it was the last chance to get hold of 51952-2004
any of the fish, for otherwise the Americans would get them in their traps on the American side in Alaska. I got hold of the evidence and, with the support of two Conservative members then in opposition, we tore the report to pieces, for the simple reason that it did not gibe with the evidence. The evidence was all the opposite way. We showed by the evidence that the fish did not run north but came south, and as a result of the representations we made the then minister announced that he would not allow the traps there. The traps remained at Sooke, however. Why? For these reasons:	The
run of salmon on the way to Fraser river, their homing ground, is through the strait of Juan de Fuca and past the headlands referred to in the neighbourhood of Sooke; then, for some unknown reason, instead of heading straight for the Fraser river, they go on to the United States side. But they do not spawn there. They go around Puget sound, running the gamut of the United States traps every few' yards, and those that are left came back to the Fraser river. It was known that the Americans were taking an enormous number. The Americans were taking 79 per cent of the total catch of fish spawned in the Fraser river. Taking the Sooke catch, the United States catch and the Fraser river catch, the Americans were said to get 70 per cent, while we were getting 30 per cent. The reason why the preceding Minister of Fisheries never cancelled the trap licences was simply this:	It was argued that as fish were
being caught in such enormous numbers on the United States side, we might as well catch what we could before they went over.
But then the situation changed. The Americans had seines, but we did not allow seines in the Fraser river and the argument was that as the Americans had seines and traps we should have seines and traps. We allowed the traps but not the seines. Then, for reasons which I need not go into, because they are not material to this argument, the people of the state of Washington got up one day and by means of the initiative got a bill passed. If it secures a sufficient number of signatories, it becomes law in spite of the legislature. They got up a bill by initiative and it went through at once. They obtained the requisite number of signatures in a few days, or at any rate, in a few weeks. That bill called for the abolition of traps in United States waters, and just about the same time we allowed seines in our waters. In other words, the conditions were reversed altogether; the tables were turned. Here was our opportunity. The Americans had taken out 219 traps-that is their own record

and the
Supply-Fisheries

query was, " Is not British Columbia going to play her part and take out the four or five she has "? Of course, the trap interests on the United States side, the capitalist interests, were keen to get their traps put back, but once the law is passed by initiative it cannot [DOT]be repealed for two years. It was brought up this spring in the legislature of the state, and the strongest argument used by those who wished to restore the United States traps was that Canada had not played the game. The Americans said that they had taken out 219 traps and Canada had not taken out the seven or eight she had. The result was so enormously to our advantage that instead of getting 30 per cent, we caught on our side 86 per cent of the total catch. It was, therefore, so very much to our interest as a nation to have removed the traps that it would have paid us to pension the forty-one men in order to ensure that the United States traps would be kept out. I met a cannery man last winter in Alberni. He said to me, " I was over in Seattle the other day where I met one of the biggest trap owners in Puget sound and he said to me he was glad that we in Canada had not taken out the traps, and they did not want us to remove them, because at the next meeting of the legislature they would use that fact as an argument in support of the restoration of the United States traps." That is why I say the conditions are different. If we do not remove our five or six traps the Americans will restore their traps.
In my letter to the minister I said:
Might I inquire what your policy in the matter is? Are you disposed to give them notice that they will not be allowed any for or beyond this year, or do you propose to refer it again to the fishery committee of the house?
I cannot see that any language could be plainer, and his answer was that he did not consider it necessary. Now I shall read the last letter, of which there are five copies in existence. The hon. member for North Vancouver has one, the Kyuoquot trollers cooperative association has one, and I have here the one sent to me. It is dated February 7, 1936, and is from the deputy minister:
Dear Mr. Neill,-
I wish to revert to your letter of June 25 last-
That would be June, 1935.
-endorsing petition by the Kyuquot trollers cooperative association urging that licences for salmon trap nets in the portion of the southwest coast of Vancouver island be discontinued.
The question has been receiving careful consideration and, in the light of all the circumstances, it has been decided to continue such licences for 1936. Notification is being given

the licensees, however, that thereafter such licences will not be granted. If trap nets are reintroduced in the state of Washington the question of reallowing them in the above area will again be reconsidered.
Trap nets have not been reintroduced in the state of Washington, and therefore it was not necessary to reconsider the question of reallowing them. The hon. member for North Vancouver, with a copy of a letter like that in his possession, is justified in saying that the fishing industry has not been treated fairly in the matter.

Will the minister inform the committee of the manner in which the recommendations of the committee have been implemented? I would ask the number of licences issued and the total revenue in the way of licence fees, and also as to what provision has been made to alter the opening in the lead of the traps in order to comply with the suggestion of the committee.

My information is that the same number was issued this year as last year and for the last few years, and the licence fee of $500 has been collected on each as recommended by the committee. As soon as the recommendation of the committee was made, an order in council was passed changing the regulations and the licence fee accordingly. Five licences were issued this year at $500 each. As to the recommendation that an opening in the lead be made, my information is that a larger opening than that recommended by the committee has been made.

Have steps been taken to ensure that those charged with the enforcement of regulations are entirely free from influence by the company? The astounding revelation was made before the committee last year that the man charged with enforcement of the fisheries regulations in connection with the traps was in the off season in the pay of the company; a very questionable situation. I should also like to know whether the department can give assurance that the regulations as they apply to operators of other types of gear are now applied to the traps. That is, when the traps are fishing for springs, are they allowed to catch sockeye in advance of the season in which other operators are allowed to spread nets for sockeye?

Regarding the statement that astounding disclosures were made before the committee last year, I think that is in line with other statements made by my hon. friend. The only astounding statement which I recollect was that apparently one poor guardian during the season when he was not

Supply-Fisheries
employed by this department had been employed by one of the companies operating traps. This year we have taken every precaution possible to see that no one who had at any time been employed with the operators of the traps would be employed as guardian.

The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) was pleased to read a long treatise from Mr. Goodrich. I am going to read a very short statement from him, made under oath on February 22, 1937. The witness C. F. Goodrich was recalled; he had been previously sworn. I will shorten it. He said he was going to read a wire received from his accountants in Victoria in regard to the set-up of his financial affairs. This is the telegram:
In accordance with instructions we have examined records of Sooke Harbour Fishing & Packing Company, Limited-
That is only one of the two concerns.

from 1918 to 1935 and find dominion income tax paid, $63,053; provincial income tax paid, $48,439 . . . paid-up capital, $24,800; surplus, $76,517. . . .
Later on, one of the committee, the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley), asked the witness, as reported at page 159 of the proceedings, whether that $25,000 represented all the money put in; "Did you put any more money in than the $25,000 of stock?" And the answer was, "No." Hon. members can get an idea of the income from the amount of income tax paid for that period. I submit it must have been substantially greater each year than the total investment of the company in the business. No wonder they are anxious to hold on.

Another question asked
by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) was whether the operators of the trap were permitted to catch one species of salmon in advance of the season. Under the rules this is not permitted. If during the cohoe season some sockeye are caught in the traps, they must be liberated.

Liberated; is that what was
done with them?
I understand it was; yes.

My information is that they
were seized by the fisheries department and given to a hospital.

If they are taken out
of the water dead, of course we cannot liberate them; it is better to give them to hospitals than to throw them back in the water. I mean, if it is possible to liberate them and save them, they are thrown back in the water.

The fact of the matter,
then, is that a trap is allowed to catch them during the close season for those classes of fish. That is the point.

The minister must be
aware that he is not on safe ground in his statement. They are not aware that sockeye salmon are caught in the trap out of season until the brail is lifted, and then it is surely impossible to liberate them; they are dead. That clearly is an admission by the minister that they are violating the regulations in a way that would be severely penalized if carried on by other fishermen. That is one of the main objections to the trap.

Surely the hon. member understands that all species of salmon in British Columbia waters do not run at the same time. It may be that during a run of one species, like cohoes or springs, a relatively few of other species may run at the same time. But if they are caught and it is possible to liberate them alive, they are liberated. If they are dead, they are given to hospitals or other charitable institutions.

Will the minister place
on record such data as have been secured in regard to the catch in the traps last season?

I am not going to speak about sockeye salmon. Seemingly it is very difficult to close the trap, whether you are fishing or talking sockeye salmon. But I did want to discuss briefly the report on the illegal fishing and canning of lobsters in the maritime provinces. I think that comes under this item. The minister will recall that last year there was appointed a commission to investigate illegal lobster fishing in the maritime provinces, particularly in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. For six weeks an investigation was carried on by a supreme court judge, Mr. Justice Le Blanc. He had with him as counsel Mr. Bridges from Moncton. Both of these men are estimable legal gentlemen, but I think the minister will agree that they know very little about lobster fishing. The impression in New Brunswick, and I think also in Prince Edward Island, where this investigation was conducted, is, that the facts which this commission undertook to obtain could very easily have been obtained by some member of the minister's department. The facts which were brought out were known by every man, woman and child in those sections. Everyone knew that there was illegal lobster fishing in New Brunswick on Northumberland strait and also on the shores of Prince Edward Island. This factfinding commission, which spent six weeks or
SuppI y-Fisheries

more in these two provinces, did not, as far as can be made out, do much but pile up a big bill.

That is the customary
thing.
The report from which the hon. gentleman is reading is the report of a commission which investigated conditions in Northumberland strait only?

And Prince Edward
Island.
It does not refer to southwest Nova Scotia.
No.
There is no such condition on the south coast of Nova Scotia.

No such condition perhaps, so far as illegal lobster fishing is concerned, but I want to say to the hon. member that if he reads his papers-and that is not necessary, because he lives there-he will find that the condition on the south coast as far as poverty and depression are concerned is as bad, if not worse than the condition in New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island.

No, not as regards illegal
fishing.

Not as to illegal fishing,
but as to poverty among the fishermen. I would advise the hon. member to visit the fishing villages, or to read the Halifax Herald, the Halifax Chronicle or any paper published on the coast. If what I am saying is not true, I shall be very much surprised. I do not wish to divert, but I could quote, for the information of the hon. member, the report of Mr. MacDonald of St. Francis Xavier university who is an authority on the matter.

He is in another part of
Nova Scotia.

He speaks for the province of Nova Scotia generally, and about the intolerable condition in the industry of the province.
But I am getting away from the point. Is the minister talcing any steps to see that the officials who are supposed to look after the guarding of the industry are men who are not engaged in poaching? I would suggest the guardians should be placed under the civil service commission. It is not fair to the men themselves, to the industry or to the provinces that the men should be recruited from the ranks of the fishermen. Then, what is done in connection with controlling the sale of lobsters to the factories in the closed season? It is a well known fact that if the factories were not allowed to buy, the fishermen would not sell. I should like to know particularly whether fisheries protection is being taken out of patronage and put under the civil service commission.

The hon. member has
been very fair in his criticism, with the exception of his opening remarks which, under the circumstances, are excusable. He started out by saying that the expenditures incurred in connection with the lobster investigation were not justified, and that an official of the department could have verified the facts just
Supply-Fisheries

as well as a royal commission. That is possible, but we must not lose sight of the circumstances under which the investigation was promoted and carried on.
Prior to the investigation we were told that the supply of live lobsters, on the coasts of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island more particularly, was gradually disappearing, and that the industry and those who lived by it were about to go out of existence. What we did was to call a conference of the packers and the fishermen, and ask them to discuss the whole matter in an effort to arrive at conclusions as to the causes of the situation. At that meeting some made allegations that the situation was caused through overfishing, illegal fishing and illegal packing. Immediately the fishermen said the allegations were not true, and the packers in turn told the fishermen that they were not doing any illegal packing or canning.
The result was that public opinion was not made aware of the facts, and in our opinion it was impossible to effect any reforms in the district. We believed that if we increased our strength and prosecuted the fishermen for violation of the law, on a large scale, we would be accused of persecuting a class of people who were in great need. We thought that in order effectively to carry out a program of reform we would have to have public opinion in our favour. We thought it was best to show the public what was going on, and that is why we appointed an independent investigator, a judge of the superior court of New Brunswick, to bring out the evidence. It was made known to the public that we would act on that evidence. That is what was done.
I believe that from that point of view the investigation was a success. Newspapers of all shades of opinion in the maritime provinces admitted at the time the investigation was in progress, and at the time they published the evidence in extenso, that no one had any idea of the extent to which illegal lobster fishing and illegal lobster canning were resorted to in that district. Not long after the investigation closed the season opened, and it was remarkable to note the change in the attitude of the public towards the question. We were enabled to change some of the officials who, we thought, were not rendering the service we expected of them; we were enabled to increase our protection; we were enabled to change the boundaries between districts 7 and 8, and enabled to close the canneries which were operating on no-man's-land, or on the dividing line between the two districts. As a result, we have testimonials in the department that in
[Mr. Michaud.!
the first season after the investigation the change in the administration was most beneficial to the fishermen of the two districts, and there was a marked evidence of the increase of lobsters in the fishing season which followed. As it happened, there were several months between the two seasons.
We were able to close the packers, the big fellows as they were called, who were taking advantage of the dire circumstances of the fishermen, who were inviting those fishermen to violate the law and offering to buy and can their catch surreptitiously. I think we have performed in that respect a great service for the fishermen. In order to enable them to carry on while they were prevented from fishing illegally, in cooperation with the governments of the provinces in which they lived we extended help, so that they may be prevented from exercising their illegal business during the closed season. Not only were we satisfied with strengthening our force and making the changes which I have just enumerated, but we carried on an educational campaign among them. We organized them into study clubs, and sent among them some educated men who placed the facts before them and showed them where they were, as the hon. member has said, killing the goose that laid the golden egg. Further, we lent them money at very moderate cost to do their own packing legally during the season. We also gave instructions to have a better class of guardian appointed to watch the fishing grounds during the closed seasons.
We have not been able to accomplish that which many people have thought would be desirable, that is, to place these temporary employees under the civil service commission, but we have seen that a thorough investigation was made by the officials of the department before the appointments were put through. We have had reports that quite a change has taken place during the last two seasons and, what is perhaps more worth while, we believe we have behind us a strong public opinion. I can assure the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that this investigation was beneficial. I believe the expenditures in connection therewith were warranted and the fishermen will receive greater benefits than they would have received by the distribution of money for temporary relief. An effort has been made to preserve their source of supply and to keep it intact in order that they may carry on the calling which they have carried on for generations back.

When such large amounts as these are going through, I think all hon. members should give way to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), otherwise all the money will slip out of the pockets of the poor people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I can understand quite clearly the desire of the Minister of Finance to have additional supply voted at this time. We have already voted one-sixth of the supply for the present year, and now we are being asked to vote another one-sixth of the main estimates for the same year. In addition, we are being asked to vote one-sixth of the supplementary estimates that have been brought down. In connection with these supplementary estimates the government finds itself in this rather unfortunate position. Bill No. 105, for the relief of unemployment, was not introduced until April 25. A year ago the estimates embodying items for purposes similar to those referred to in Bill No. 105 were introduced on March 12. When Bill No. 105 was before the house hon. members were insistent in their demands for information as to the amounts to be expended, the nature of the undertakings and other particulars. This information was not forthcoming. We were told that we had to wait for the supplementary estimates.
In looking over these supplementary estimates it is to be noted that the total is $106,509,436.10, a large amount. However, upon examination we find that government owned enterprises require $44,413,714, leaving
about $61,000,000 for all other purposes. As a rule, the main estimates are smaller than those of last year. When one goes through these supplementary estimates one of the striking features is the large number of items that might very well have been included in the main estimates and which, in the ordinary course of events, would have been there. We find page after page of items covering public buildings which should have been brought down in the main estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They never have been.

I would say that larger amounts have been brought down in the main estimates than is the case this year. As the minister says, we have always had supplementary estimates for public buildings, harbour improvements and so on; but with the experience of the last few years and the necessity of initiating work for the relief of unemployment as early in the season as possible, I do suggest that the government should have been in a position to include in the main estimates a larger number of these items than they did. I am not complaining that they are there, but the fact appears to be that these items have been included to swell the amount of money made available for the alleviation of unemployment under Bill No. 105. When you deduct the amounts I have mentioned from this large total of the main estimates; when you consider the items that should have been included in the main estimates, the remainder is not so large after all. I hope it will be sufficient for the purposes, but I have my doubts.
As I have said, it is unfortunate that these estimates were not before the house when we were considering Bill No. 105. The items are scattered through this rather bulky volume of supplementary estimates, and we shall desire to discuss them in the light of the provisions of Bill No. 105. We shall want to point out where we believe they are inadequate or where we consider they are not exactly suitable to existing conditions, where they do not go far enough or where perhaps the expenditure is not, as we believe, in the public interest or best calculated to accomplish the purposes outlined in Bill No. 105. I say it is unfortunate that we have not had that opportunity earlier in the session and that this amount of money was not available earlier in *the season.	[DOT]
For these reasons, and while reserving all rights to discuss any of these items and to object to any of them, I feel that at this stage we are bound to comply with the request of the minister for this grant of one-sixth of these supplementary estimates; but as I
Interim Supply Bill

have said, it must be without any prejudice whatever to the conditions that we have made in connection with Bill No. 105 and without waiver of any rights that we might have exercised if these estimates had been brought down much earlier and we had had ample opportunity to discuss them in the light of the provisions of Bill No. 105.
With these reservations, I have not anything further to say on the minister's motion for one-sixth of the supply in the supplementary estimates, and what I have said with regard to those would apply with equal force to the criticisms which we may desire to make of any other items that are not in any way related to the program outlined in Bill No. 105.

speechtext:
I am sorry my hon. friend got the wrong impression from what I said.
I said that we would be going back into supply, but the Minister of Fisheries has just advised that he has no hope of getting the item through to-night and that progress might be made in agriculture. The Minister of Fisheries does not wish to go on immediately, and the Minister of Agriculture is ready.

Looking over these items in detail, one is struck by the large number of items that are simply supplementary to the regular administrative items of the department. I find: Departmental administration, further amount required, $7,350; publicity and extension division, further amount required, $5,640; then, passing over the next four items under the heading "special," we come to the heading, "marketing services," and we find a further amount required of $7,000 odd for agricultural economics. speechtext: Generally speaking, to answer the last question first, the amounts that were in special estimates last year are under the heading " special " in these estimates on page one; that is, such amounts as were voted for paying freight on live stock and paying feed and fodder, and providing resettlement and prairie farm rehabilitation. In pamphlet form?

Well, there will be articles to the press in connection with agriculture generally, but also pamphlets.
How has this work been done in the past?
There has been a certain amount of it done, but it is a growing activity in the department and two additional men are required for it.
How is the mailing list for these publications prepared?

No; the space in the

Are there to be new publications sent out, or are we to continue with just the publications we have now?

How many of these
publicity editors will the department have when these two are added? Are they appointed by the civil service commission?

My experience leads me to believe that objections have been raised in some areas. Could the minister tell me what the objections have been to the establishment of restricted areas. I have in mind one county which has raised considerable protest.

There are very few objections made to the establishment of these areas, but where it is made it is usually by those who are raising cattle for beef purposes. Very seldom do we have objection from those raising cattle for dairy purposes. The other evening I read into Hansard a statement showing the results in a great many districts. If the hon. member would turn up Hansard, on the date our main estimates were before the committee, he would find a statement indicating that great progress had been made in the matter of eliminating tuberculosis from all those areas.

I have read the statement referred to by the minister. There are still some areas where it is proposed to put these regulations into effect, and some objection is made, more particularly to the rates of compensation. Would it be possible to increase the compensation?

I can quite understand that where an animal valued at from $200 to $300 is slaughtered and the owner receives no more than $150, there would be cause for complaint. However, the department has always taken the position that where an individual allows tuberculosis to develop in his herd he should assume some responsibility. The limit of compensation has been set at $150, and it has been found over many years that this is accepted fairly generally as liberal compensation.

It might be of interest to some hon. members from agricultural districts to know the experience I had in connection *with tuberculosis. In 1921 I had a herd of pure bred cattle which were tested for tuberculosis, and I lost almost $6,000 worth. The last animal reacted in 1922; my herd is still under the dominion government accredited plan, and I have had no reactors since. Apparently the serums Used are perfect. At that time the maximum compensation allowed

was $160. I lost several animals ranging in value from $1,000 down to $400, but I was perfectly satisfied with the settlement. As the minister has said, I felt that I should accept some responsibility for the fact that I had a herd with a number of tubercular animals in it, and I have never regretted having cleaned up my herd at that time. My advice to anyone who has not had his herd tested is to do so without delay and come under the dominion government accredited plan.
